title: Normal Sinus Rhythm
subject: Medicine
summary: Normal sinus rhythm (NSR) is the heart's regular electrical pattern originating from the sino‑atrial node. Recognising NSR and its variations guides diagnosis of arrhythmias and informs urgent management in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: NSR is a regular rhythm with a rate of 60‑100 bpm, each P wave preceding a QRS complex, PR interval 0.12‑0.20 s, and consistent QRS morphology.
b: P wave before every QRS
PR interval 0.12‑0.20 s
Rate 60‑100 bpm
Regular R‑R intervals

sections.p: NSR itself is not staged; severity relates to underlying disease (e.g., heart failure) that may alter rate or rhythm stability.
b: Stable NSR – no symptoms, normal vitals
Tachy‑NSR (>100 bpm) – may indicate fever, anemia, hyperthyroidism
Brady‑NSR (<60 bpm) – may reflect high vagal tone or drug effect

sections.p: NSR is the default rhythm; deviations arise from reversible or chronic conditions common in low‑resource settings.
b: Fever, malaria, sepsis – raise rate
Anemia, sickle‑cell crisis – tachycardia
Hypothyroidism, beta‑blockers – bradycardia
Electrolyte disturbances (K+, Mg2+) – may precipitate blocks

sections.p: Patients with NSR are usually asymptomatic; any symptoms usually stem from the underlying cause rather than the rhythm itself.
b: Palpitations only if rate is at extremes
Dizziness if bradycardic with low output
Chest pain if tachycardia from infection

t.b: Confirms rhythm origin and rate; normal P‑QRS‑T pattern indicates NSR
Correlates heart rate with ECG; ensures peripheral perfusion
Detects anemia or infection that may explain tachycardia
Identifies hypo‑ or hyper‑thyroidism affecting rate
Finds K+ or Mg2+ abnormalities that predispose to arrhythmias

sections.p: While NSR itself is benign, rapid change in rate or loss of NSR signals impending instability.
b: Sudden tachycardia >130 bpm with hypotension – possible sepsis shock
Bradycardia <40 bpm with syncope – high‑grade AV block
NSR with absent pulse – pulseless electrical activity (PEA) arrest

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause; maintain NSR with supportive measures.
b: Treat infection (antibiotics, antimalarials) to lower tachycardia
Correct anemia with transfusion or iron where indicated
Adjust medications: reduce beta‑blocker dose if bradycardic
IV fluids for hypovolemia; monitor electrolytes

sections.p: Re‑assess rhythm after treating the precipitant; educate patients on signs needing urgent review.
b: Repeat ECG after fever resolves
Monitor heart rate during chronic disease follow‑up (HIV, TB)
Encourage hydration and malaria prophylaxis in endemic areas

sections.p: Conditions that mimic NSR on bedside assessment.
b: Sinus tachycardia – same origin but rate >100 bpm
Sinus bradycardia – rate <60 bpm
Atrial flutter with 2:1 block – regular but saw‑tooth flutter waves

sections.p: Pitfalls in interpreting rhythm and related tests.
b: Artifact on ECG may look like regular P‑QRS pattern – verify with pulse
Low‑output states can give weak pulses despite NSR – check capillary refill
Electrolyte normalisation may not restore NSR if structural disease present

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of pulse despite ECG showing NSR
Heart rate >130 bpm with systolic BP <90 mmHg
Bradycardia <40 bpm with syncope or altered mental status

faq.q: Is sinus rhythm always safe in heart failure?
faq.a: Yes, NSR is preferred because it provides atrial contribution to ventricular filling, but rate control may still be needed.

faq.q: Can a patient be in NSR and still be unstable?
faq.a: Yes, if the underlying cause (e.g., severe sepsis) causes hypotension or poor perfusion despite a regular rhythm.

faq.q: What if an ECG machine is unavailable?
faq.a: Use a pulse check and bedside cardiac auscultation; a regular rhythm with a palpable pulse strongly suggests NSR.

exam: A febrile malaria patient has a heart rate of 115 bpm; what is the next step? — Assess for NSR on ECG, treat malaria, and monitor for dehydration‑related tachycardia.
You see a regular rhythm on monitor but no peripheral pulse; what does this indicate? — Pulseless electrical activity; start CPR and look for reversible causes.
How would you differentiate sinus tachycardia from atrial flutter with 2:1 block on a limited ECG? — Look for saw‑tooth flutter waves; sinus tachycardia has distinct P waves before each QRS.
A patient on chronic beta‑blocker presents with a heart rate of 48 bpm and dizziness; what is your management? — Review medication dose, consider temporary hold, and monitor ECG for NSR stability.
In a resource‑limited ward, which single test gives the most information about rhythm and rate? — A 12‑lead ECG, if unavailable use a pulse‑oximeter waveform and manual pulse count.
Why is NSR preferred over atrial fibrillation in patients with left‑ventricular dysfunction? — NSR preserves atrial kick, improving cardiac output and reducing symptoms.
A child with sickle‑cell disease presents with tachycardia; what causes should you prioritize? — Pain, anemia, infection, and possible hypovolemia; treat underlying trigger and reassess rhythm.
What red‑flag sign would make you call for urgent senior review in a patient with NSR? — New onset hypotension, altered mental status, or loss of peripheral pulse.
